summary.summary:
Single-actor recon campaign from 192.168.92.129 against host co1508kali2 (192.168.92.131), spanning ~09:51Z to ~10:04Z on 2026-10-27, all three logs (firewall.log, access.log, ssh.log) correlate on the same clock (UTC).

Phase 1 - Port scan (09:51:17Z - 10:03:24Z, firewall.log): 192.168.92.129 sent a long, steady stream of single SYN packets from a handful of rotating source ports (53372, 56818, 36713, 36715, 36718, 36720...) to a huge spread of destination ports on 192.168.92.131 (22, 222, 2288, 2251, 2222, 22939, 2200, 64680, 2601, 2702, 8888, 443, 993, 8080, 256, etc.), with varying TTLs (64, 58, 55, 46, 37...) on the probes after the initial batch - consistent with a scripted/automated TCP SYN scanner (e.g., nmap -sS) using randomized or forged TTLs, enumerating services including SSH on both standard (22) and non-standard high ports. No corresponding completed connections appear in ssh.log at these times for most ports, confirming these are scan probes, not real sessions.

Phase 2 - Web fingerprinting (10:03:31Z, access.log): Once port 80 was confirmed open, 192.168.92.129 ran basic fingerprinting requests: `GET /` with both HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1, and a `PROPFIND /` with User-Agent "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Nmap Scripting Engine...)" - classic nmap HTTP NSE script behavior to grab banners/headers. A `robots.txt` pull (10:03:46Z) with UA "ai-recon-agent (study tool)" followed, consistent with a scripted recon tool enumerating standard disclosure files.

Phase 3 - Directory/content brute force (10:03:46Z - 10:04:56Z, access.log): Massive brute-force directory enumeration (14,558 requests total, 14,204 of them 404) using gobuster/3.8.2 and "Fuzz Faster U Fool" (ffuf) wordlists, hitting admin panel names, CMS paths, backup directories, and credential/history files (/admin, /phpmyadmin, /wp-login, /.git/HEAD, /admin/.ssh, /admin/.bash_history, /backup/*, etc.). Two paths returned HTTP 200: `/admin/` (hit twice - once by "ai-recon-agent (study tool)" at 10:03:57Z, once by gobuster/3.8.2 at 10:03:59Z) and `/backup/index.html` (10:04:38Z by ai-recon-agent). These 200s mean a real, enumerable admin directory and backup directory exist on the server and were discovered by the brute-forcer - this is the most actionable finding, as these paths may expose sensitive functionality or data.

Phase 4 - SSH noise (10:03:25Z - 10:03:36Z, ssh.log): During the same window as the port scan hitting port 22, sshd on the target logged repeated "OpenSSL version mismatch. Built against 30000090, you have 30600050" errors (PIDs 21609, 21658-21660, 21702) - these are not authentication failures but library-version warnings thrown when sshd handles unusual/rapid incoming connection attempts, timing-correlated with the SYN scan's probes to port 22. auth_summary found zero failed logins and zero successful logins recorded in ssh.log - there is no evidence of actual credential brute-forcing or a successful SSH logon in the provided ssh.log; it only contains service-start and these mismatch-warning lines, so this is reconnaissance/pre-positioning, not confirmed compromise.

Overall narrative: 192.168.92.129 conducted a fully automated, multi-tool recon chain (raw SYN scan -> nmap NSE HTTP probe -> gobuster/ffuf content discovery) against 192.168.92.131 in under 15 minutes, discovered a live /admin/ and /backup/ web path, and generated sshd noise while scanning port 22, but no evidence in the supplied logs shows a successful authentication or follow-on exploitation. This looks like the reconnaissance/weaponization-staging phase of an attack, not yet a breach.

findings.title: TCP SYN port scan against 192.168.92.131 from 192.168.92.129
findings.recommendation: Confirm with the firewall/host owner whether this is an authorized scan (lab exercise) or hostile recon. If unauthorized, block/rate-limit 192.168.92.129 at the perimeter and alert on any future SYN sweep from this host.

findings.title: Nmap NSE HTTP fingerprinting against web server
findings.recommendation: Treat as confirmation the scanning host moved from network-layer to application-layer recon; correlate with WAF/IDS alerts if available and watch for follow-up exploit attempts from the same source.

findings.title: Directory/file brute force with gobuster and ffuf against web root
findings.recommendation: Rate-limit or block repeat 404-heavy clients, deploy a WAF rule for gobuster/ffuf user-agents, and review web server logs for any successful hits beyond the two identified below.

findings.title: Real /admin/ and /backup/ paths discovered and returned HTTP 200 during brute force
findings.recommendation: Immediately audit what /admin/ and /backup/ expose (authentication requirements, directory listing, sensitive backup files). Remove or restrict public access, require authentication, and verify no credentials or source code are exposed under /backup/.

findings.title: sshd OpenSSL version-mismatch errors coincident with port-22 scan traffic
findings.evidence: 2026-10-27T10:03:31+0000 co1508kali2 sshd[21658]: OpenSSL version mismatch. Built against 30000090, you have 30600050
findings.recommendation: These are library warnings, not auth failures - patch/rebuild sshd against the matching OpenSSL version to eliminate log noise, and separately confirm no actual authentication attempts exist in the real production auth log (this ssh.log sample contains no failed/successful login entries to analyze with auth_summary).

next_steps: Confirm with the system/lab owner whether 192.168.92.129 is an authorized pentest/scanner box; if not, block it at the firewall.

Pull the actual production auth.log (not the 9-line sample) for host 192.168.92.131 around 10:03-10:05Z on 2026-10-27 and re-run auth_summary to rule out any successful SSH logon that followed the scan.
Manually browse (from an isolated/authorized vantage point) to confirm what /admin/ and /backup/ currently serve, and check web server config for directory listing and access controls.
Search web server logs for any other IPs reusing the same ai-recon-agent/gobuster/ffuf user-agents in case this is a shared red-team tool used elsewhere.
If this is a live production system, rotate credentials for anything reachable from /admin/ and remove /backup/ from the public document root.

Add detection rules (IDS/WAF) for the specific scanner UAs and the rapid-fire 404 pattern seen here, and for SYN sweeps touching more than N distinct destination ports from one source in under a minute.
